records.found: One peer-reviewed paper dated in the window bears on this treatment: on 2026-11-05 Cell Stem Cell published work in which a DNA-methylation epigenome editor, delivered as RNA with no cut in the DNA, silenced a chosen gene in human blood-making stem cells, and the silencing lasted four months after the cells were put into mice and could be partly undone by a demethylating editor. That is cells treated outside the body, not a person or a whole living animal given the treatment, so it does not meet the test. The hepatitis B trial named in the record (registry number NCT06671093) was last updated on 2026-01-06, still shows recruiting, and still posts no results, and the company's own news page carries nothing after 2026-05-30.

findings.what: Cell Stem Cell paper: an RNA-delivered DNA-methylation editor silenced the platelet gene ITGB3 in human blood-making stem cells without cutting the DNA; the silencing survived self-renewal and differentiation, was still stable four months after the cells were transplanted into mice, and was partly reversed by targeted demethylation.

The registry entry for the hepatitis B epigenetic silencer trial (NCT06671093) was last updated on 2026-01-06: status recruiting, start 2024-11-29 (actual), estimated enrolment 36, primary completion estimated 2028-06-28, no results posted. Nothing changed inside the window, so the conference result of 2026-05-30 is still not a peer-reviewed report or posted registry result.

records.found: Two things dated in the window bear on the test, both against rather than for. On 2026-10-29 GeroScience published a secondary analysis of the large aspirin trial in older adults: epigenetic clocks were used to validate a measure of everyday capacity, and daily aspirin did not prevent functional decline (in women it went with a slightly faster decline). On 2026-11-04 a preprint of a 848-person placebo-controlled trial of a buckwheat sprout powder reported that its exploratory readings of epigenetic age in 34 people gave signals that did not survive correction for multiple testing. Neither is a treatment turning a validated clock back, so the stage does not move; separately, the larger follow-up trial the record names (NCT04375657) is still unchanged since 2025-05-07 with a primary completion date of 2025-12 now almost a year past.

findings.what: GeroScience paper (secondary analysis of a randomised trial of 100 mg daily aspirin against placebo in 18,581 people aged 65 and over): a four-part capacity score correlated with epigenetic clocks including PC-PhenoAge, PC-GrimAge and DunedinPACE, but aspirin did not slow functional decline and women on aspirin declined slightly faster. The clocks are used to validate the measure, not as a treatment outcome.

Preprint of a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 18 g a day of Himalayan Tartary buckwheat sprout powder for 12 weeks (848 randomised, 662 analysed): the main measure of thinking did not differ from placebo, and exploratory readings of epigenetic age in 34 people gave only hypothesis-generating signals, none surviving correction for multiple testing. It is a preprint, not a peer-reviewed report.

The registry entry for the larger thymus-regrowth follow-up trial (NCT04375657, sponsor Intervene Immune, 85 people estimated) is unchanged since 2025-05-07: still recruiting, start 2020-11-23, primary completion still given as 2025-12, no results posted. Read live on 2026-11-09, so the record's observation of 2026-10-17 still holds and the stated completion date is now about eleven months past.

records.found: Three company reports dated in the window show the amyloid antibodies selling much faster than a year ago, which bears on the wide-use rung without meeting it. On 2026-10-28 Biogen reported that worldwide sales of lecanemab in the quarter to 2026-09-30 were $202 million, 67 per cent more than the $121 million a year earlier, with $107 million of it in the United States; Eisai's own notice of the same date gives 61.5 billion yen for the six months to 2026-09-30 against 41.1 billion a year earlier. On 2026-10-29 Eli Lilly reported sales of the second antibody (donanemab) of about $193 million in the quarter, 175 per cent more than a year earlier. Which way it cuts: faster, towards the earlier end of the wide-use range, because sales are roughly doubling year on year and the first full quarter of the at-home autoinjector is only now being sold; but none of the three gives a count of people treated or of people eligible, so the test for wide use still cannot be checked, and on 2026-10-30 Eisai said the five-year results from the main trial's open-label extension will only be presented on 2026-11-16, after the window.

findings.what: Biogen's third-quarter results release: worldwide in-market sales of lecanemab of $202 million for the quarter to 2026-09-30, up 67 per cent from $121 million a year earlier, of which $107 million in the United States; Biogen's own share of the partnership $68.4 million. No count of people treated, and nothing on how many of them use the at-home autoinjector.

Eisai's preliminary revenue notice for lecanemab: 61.5 billion yen worldwide for the six months to 2026-09-30 against 41.1 billion yen a year earlier, of which 32.5 billion in the United States, 13.0 billion in Japan and 9.7 billion in China. No patient counts; full figures were due on 2026-11-10.

Eli Lilly's third-quarter results: sales of the second amyloid antibody (donanemab, sold as Kisunla) of about $193 million, 175 per cent more than the same quarter of 2025. Figure taken from reporting of the results, not from the release itself.

Eisai's notice that five-year results from the open-label continuation of the main lecanemab trial, and a set of real-world reports three years after approval, will be presented at a conference running 2026-11-16 to 2026-11-19 in Boston. No figures given, and the presentations fall after this window.

A paper in a German neurology journal discussing why the German benefit assessment found no added benefit for donanemab although the regulator approved it, and reporting that a more strictly defined subgroup analysis confirmed a benefit over placebo. records.found: Four records dated in the window bear on the wide-use rung. On 2026-11-03 Circulation published the one-year open-label continuation of the main trial of the gene silencer vutrisiran in this disease: among 466 people who carried on, those on the drug throughout had a 37 per cent lower risk of death from any cause than those who started it late. On 2026-11-02 Clinical Research in Cardiology reported the first real-world use of the newer stabiliser acoramidis in Germany, 289 people in six months, median age 82, 86 per cent of them starting it as their first treatment. On 2026-11-03 Pfizer reported that its older stabiliser family (tafamidis) sold $1,773 million in the quarter, 11 per cent more than a year before, which it put down to more people being diagnosed, and on 2026-10-29 BridgeBio reported $253.2 million for acoramidis, about 134 per cent more than a year earlier. Which way it cuts: faster, towards the earliest wide-use year of 2027, because three drugs are now selling into the same disease and diagnosis is spreading; against that, none of the four gives a count or share of eligible patients, which is what the test asks for, and the German paper's 289 people over six months is a reminder how few are reached.

findings.what: Circulation paper on the one-year open-label continuation of the HELIOS-B trial of vutrisiran in transthyretin heart disease: of 654 people in the main trial, 466 continued; those on the drug throughout had a 37 per cent lower risk of a first cardiovascular event or death and a 37 per cent lower risk of death from any cause than those switched from placebo, with health status and heart strain markers preserved through month 48 and no new safety signals.

Clinical Research in Cardiology paper (StarTTR) on the first real-world use of acoramidis in Germany: 289 people with at least one prescription between April and September 2025, median age 82, 15 per cent women, 86 per cent treatment-naive, 87 per cent started in hospital outpatient clinics. The authors call it an early benchmark for watching how fast the drug is taken up.

Pfizer's third-quarter results: the tafamidis family (Vyndaqel, Vyndamax, Vynmac) sold $1,773 million in the quarter, up 11 per cent as reported and 12 per cent operationally, which the company attributes to continued market expansion in the United States and to more patients being diagnosed internationally plus better access in some markets. No count of people treated or eligible.

BridgeBio's third-quarter results: $253.2 million of United States sales of acoramidis in the quarter, about 134 per cent more than a year earlier, growth again led by people starting treatment for the first time; approved in the United States, European Union, Japan, Switzerland, Brazil, the United Kingdom and Australia. Unlike a year earlier, the release gives no count of prescriptions or prescribers. It also reports the first person dosed in a 36-month study of heart structure and function, and a deposit-clearing antibody (BBP-717) nominated with a filing planned for 2027.

records.found: Two peer-reviewed reports dated in the window bear on this treatment, one for and one against. On 2026-10-23 Aging Cell published work in which old mice given the resetting genes in short bursts, then stopped, suffered less brain damage after a stroke: smaller damaged area at 48 hours, better neurological scores and tightrope performance, preserved myelin and more nerve-insulating cells, against untreated controls. On 2026-10-27 the journal Aging published a reanalysis of gene-activity data from the liver, kidney and spleen of old mice given seven months of the same treatment: ageing inflammation was suppressed in liver and kidney, but the spleen showed heavy cell division and DNA-repair activity, which the authors read as a possible risk of sustained genetic and growth stress. Which way it cuts: the stroke work adds another restored function in a living animal and supports the earlier end of the first-human range; the reanalysis speaks to the tumour worry behind the latest year, and the authors ask for larger controlled studies, so the far end of the range should not narrow.

findings.what: Aging Cell paper (Mallavibarrena and colleagues): aged mice in which the four resetting genes were switched on in short cycles had, 48 hours after an artery in the brain was blocked, a significantly smaller damaged area than untreated controls, with better neurological scores and tightrope performance, preserved myelin, more total and precursor insulating cells, preserved nerve-cell density and less scarring activity.

Aging (Albany) paper (Meiners and colleagues) reanalysing gene-activity data from liver, kidney and spleen of aged mice given seven months of the same brief-burst resetting: age-related immune and inflammatory activity was suppressed and metabolic activity restored in liver and kidney, while the spleen showed cell-cycle, DNA-replication and damage-response activity with more of one blood-progenitor cell type and fewer natural killer cells, which the authors flag as a possible risk of sustained genetic and growth stress; they call for larger controlled studies on safety.

unmatched.what: The registry posted results for a late-stage trial of an antibody against the other Alzheimer's protein, tau (posdinemab, NCT04619420). The trial is marked terminated, with the reason given as the drug not reaching statistical significance in slowing clinical decline.
unmatched.why_it_matters: A failed tau antibody is a result that counts against the broader idea that clearing an age-related protein deposit changes the course of a disease; the site tracks the amyloid antibodies but has no entry for the tau ones, and this is the kind of failure that sets the pace of the field.

unmatched.what: A new late-stage trial of a third amyloid antibody (trontinemab) in people with no symptoms yet but at risk of them was posted as recruiting (NCT07717411).
unmatched.why_it_matters: Treating people before symptoms is the step that would turn these drugs from a late treatment into something closer to prevention, which is a different question from the one the amyloid entry asks.

unmatched.what: Reporting of a Nature Biotechnology paper (published 2026-09-07) in which six clocks built from blood proteins all read a lower biological age in people given the anti-fibrosis drug rentosertib in a 12-week early-stage trial, with the authors noting that protein clocks alone cannot separate ageing effects from disease effects.
unmatched.why_it_matters: It is a treatment moving a measured age reading in people, which is the shape of the question the site's clock entries ask, but the clock is read from blood proteins rather than the chemical marks on DNA, so it fits neither this packet's clock treatment nor its branch; the records already hold the paper under another entry.
